title: MROUND and FLOOR: round to a multiple

screens.prompt: Round each pallet's unit count to the nearest five and put the first one in C2.

hints.syntax: =MROUND(B2,5): the number first, the multiple second.
hints.func-mround: The target here is a multiple of five, so name the five in the second argument.
hints.require-ref: Read the count from B2, so the second pallet gets its own answer in C3.
hints.value: 47 sits two units above 45 and three below 50, so 45 is nearer.
hints.error: The grader flags FLOOR in this mode: it reaches 45 by always going down, so it only agrees while the count is nearer the lower multiple.

reject.why: rounds to the nearest whole number, 47, which is not a multiple of five
the right answer from the wrong direction — 45 here, but FLOOR never rounds up
the count typed in, so the second pallet keeps the first pallet's rounding
rounds to the nearest ten, 50, so the packs no longer line up with the fives
division by zero, so the cell holds #DIV/0!
the missing comma means the arguments never separate

screens.prompt: Only whole packs ship, so put the units that fit the full packs of the first order into D2.

hints.syntax: =FLOOR(B2,C2): the number first, then the pack size to fill.
hints.func-floor: Only whole packs ship, so drop the part pack instead of rounding to the nearest one.
hints.require-ref: Read units and pack size from B2 and C2, so the second order is calculated the same way.
hints.value: 47 units fill seven packs of six, which is 42, and 5 units are left over.
hints.error: A figure above 47 means CEILING or MROUND: the shipment cannot exceed the units ordered.

reject.why: rounds the pack count to nearest, 48, and commits to a pack nobody filled
rounds up, 48, which is the opposite direction from what ships
the units typed in, so the second order is never actually calculated
rounds to a multiple of one, which leaves the count untouched at 47
rounds down to a multiple of four, 44, using a pack size the supplier never offered
division by zero, so the cell holds #DIV/0!
the missing comma leaves two arguments jammed into one

docs.explain:
MROUND takes a number and the multiple to land on, so =MROUND(B2,5) asks which multiple of five is nearest to 47. The answer is 45, because 45 is two away and 50 is three away. FLOOR takes the same second argument and always moves down.

The second screen packs in sixes and ships only full packs. =FLOOR(B2,C2) returns 42, which is seven packs, and the five units left over do not fill another. MROUND in that column would return 48 and bill for a pack that was never filled.

Keep the pack size in a cell, not in the formula. A supplier moving from sixes to eights changes one value, where a typed 6 has to be found in every row. MROUND also needs the number and the multiple to share a sign, or it returns #NUM!.

errors.text: The multiple is zero, and zero gives MROUND no grid of multiples to land on.
The number and the multiple have different signs, so MROUND cannot choose a multiple between them.
MROUND where FLOOR is needed returns 48 and promises a pack nobody filled.

docs.atWork: A warehouse that ships whole packs, and a price list quoted in five-pence steps, where the multiple is part of the calculation.
docs.outcome: Round to a pack size or a price step instead of to a number of decimals.
docs.dataset: Pallet counts and order lines packed in sixes

seo.title: MROUND and FLOOR in Excel
seo.description: ROUND asks how many decimals to keep. MROUND and FLOOR ask which multiple a number belongs to: cartons of six, pallets of forty-eight, price steps of five.
